newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends lower on cash, more supply.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends lower on cash, more supply.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures finished sharply lower Tuesday on mild weather in the West, weakness in the region's cash power market and rising output from the San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station (SONGS).
"You're seeing some convergence between cash and futures," a futures trader said, noting that the August power contracts will expire Monday July 28.
August Palo Verde (PV) futures settled down $1.66 at $33.80 a megawatt hour (MWh), 15 cents above its session low.
September PV finished down $1.20 at $27.36. Deferred PV contracts ended 25 to 80 cents lower.
August California-Oregon Border (COB) settled down 72 cents at $20.46 after sinking to a session low at $20.25.
September COB finished down 70 cents at $21.02. Other active COB months ended 15 to 35 cents lower.
Firm, peak power prices for Wednesday at PV dropped to $29.00-32.00 a MWh from Monday's $36.00-41.00, and those at COB were flat at $17.00-18.00.
The 1,070 megawatt (MW) SONGS unit 2 and 1,080 MW SONGS unit 3, in San Clemente, California, were both operating at 70 percent power midday Tuesday, the operator Southern California Edison Co said.
Concerns over the operating status of the SONGS units last week buoyed August futures last week.
Market sources said they expect the power complex to test lower levels ahead of August's expiration Monday if western physical power prices continue to fall.
"Given Monday's expiration, I think we have a little more downside to go," a Houston futures trader said.
Analysts said they expect August PV to test technical support at $31.25 and August COB $20.00.
If futures were to rebound, August PV would likely fill the a chart gap created today at $33.60-35.25 and August COB $20.50-21.15, market sources said.
Meterologists called for seasonal summer temperatures across most of the West into next week.

Coastal cities from Seattle to Los Angeles were forecast to see readings in the 70s Fahrenheit, while interior centers in Southwest like Phoenix and Las Vegas were expected to hit the 100 degree mark later this week.
Separately, the Western Systems Coordinating Council was tentatively set to vote this week on raising the capacity of the Pacific Intertie transmission system to 6,900 MW from 6,300 MW.
